question.text: A person uses a boat to travel across a flowing river to the opposite bank. To cross in the least possible time, the journey takes 10 min, resulting in a downstream displacement of 120 m. If the crossing is instead made along the shortest possible route straight across the stream, the trip takes 12.5 min. Calculate the following quantities:

parts.label: b
parts.asks: the boat's velocity relative to the water

parts.label: c
parts.asks: the flow speed of the current

conditions: constant boat speed relative to water
drift during minimum time crossing = 120 m

solution.approach: The minimum-time crossing uses the boat's full speed across the bank; the shortest-path crossing uses the speed left after cancelling the current, giving two equations for width and boat speed.

steps.text: In the minimum-time crossing the boat heads straight across, so the width equals boat speed times 10 min, and the current speed follows from the drift in that same time.
steps.equation: d = v_b × 10 min; v_r = 120 m / 10 min = 12 m/min

steps.text: In the shortest-path crossing the boat angles upstream so its resultant path is straight across; the effective crossing speed is reduced by the current.
Equate the two expressions for the width and solve for the boat speed.
Substitute the boat speed back to find the width, and state all three results.
steps.equation: d = 10 min × 20 m/min = 200 m; v_b = 20 m/min ≈ 0.33 m/s; v_r = 12 m/min = 0.2 m/s

final_answer.value: (a) width = 200 m, (b) boat speed relative to water = 20 m/min ≈ 0.33 m/s, (c) current speed = 12 m/min = 0.2 m/s

common_mistakes.text: Dividing the 120 m drift by the 12.5 min shortest-path time instead of the 10 min minimum-time gives a wrong current speed of 9.6 m/min instead of 12 m/min.
Writing the shortest-path speed as v_b − v_r instead of √(v_b² − v_r²) gives a wrong boat speed of 60 m/min.
